record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: What particle-scale simulations of dense suspensions and dilute gels are needed to reproduce the experimentally observed nonlinear wall-friction laws and to explain the multiscale physics of wall slip, including lubrication forces, particle elasticity, and non-local plasticity?

evidence.quote: Yet, more work is needed, especially at the particle scale, to capture the non-linearity of the friction laws reported experimentally [see Fig. 4(c)]. In particular, molecular dynamic simulations of dense suspensions, as well as dilute gels, which would help understand the multiscale physics at stake in wall slip, are still sorely lacking.

artifact.category_tag: wall slip in soft amorphous materials
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a dense suspension (a high–volume-fraction assembly of rigid or weakly deformable spherical particles immersed in a Newtonian solvent) or a dilute colloidal gel (a sparse, percolated network of attractive Brownian particles) confined between two smooth or patterned solid walls and subjected to simple shear. Experiments report that, near the walls, the macroscopic slip velocity v_s and the wall shear stress σ_w obey a nonlinear friction law of the form σ_w = f(v_s) with f strongly nonlinear (e.g., power-law or saturating), rather than the linear Navier relation σ_w = k v_s. The microscopic mechanisms believed to contribute include (i) hydrodynamic lubrication forces between particles and the wall, (ii) elastic deformation of individual particles and of the contact zone, and (iii) non-local plastic rearrangements in the bulk that couple to the near-wall region through a cooperativity length.

Construct a particle-scale dynamical model (for instance a molecular-dynamics-type scheme with explicit lubrication interactions, Hertzian or JKR contact elasticity, Brownian forces, and, for gels, short-range attractive potentials together with a non-local fluidity or plasticity coupling) for such confined systems, and prove or demonstrate the following:

1. In the dense-suspension regime, the simulated steady-state relation between σ_w and v_s reproduces the experimentally observed nonlinear wall-friction law, and identify which combination of lubrication, particle elasticity, and bulk non-local plasticity is responsible for each regime of the curve.

2. In the dilute-gel regime, the same class of models reproduces the corresponding nonlinear slip law and quantitatively predicts the dependence of the slip length and slip velocity on volume fraction, attraction strength, and wall roughness.

3. Derive, from these particle-scale simulations, a coarse-grained constitutive boundary condition relating σ_w, v_s, and bulk rheological variables that captures the multiscale physics of wall slip in both systems.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction: particle-scale (molecular-dynamics-type) simulations of dense suspensions and dilute gels that reproduce the experimentally observed nonlinear wall-friction laws and explain the multiscale physics of wall slip are described as "sorely lacking." No subsequent work was found that comprehensively delivers such simulations and the corresponding coarse-grained boundary condition; partial progress exists on lubrication-resolved suspension simulations and on non-local fluidity models, but a unified particle-scale account remains absent.

status_evidence.title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials
status_evidence.snippet: Molecular dynamic simulations of dense suspensions, as well as dilute gels, which would help understand the multiscale physics at stake in wall slip, are still sorely lacking.
status_evidence.claim: The need for such particle-scale simulations is stated as an open problem.
